title: Sayings and idioms
job: The figurative everyday, and when it is used
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A fixed expression is repeated, never composed. The forty modules before this one taught sentences you build; these items are strings you store whole and produce unchanged, word for word and in one order.

The body idiom is an iḍāfa L3 already opened — khafīf ad-damm, ṭawīl al-bāl, ṭawīl al-lisān: an adjective in front of a definite body part. The grammar is old; what is new is that the whole means what no part of it says.

Read word by word, khafīf ad-damm is a blood disorder and ṭawīl al-lisān is a measurement. Literal reading fails in both directions — an English idiom carried straight across into Arabic is nonsense too.

man inside a proverb is not L2-M7's question word who. In man jadda wajada it is a free relative — whoever strove, found — a fossil that survives only inside sayings. Recognise it; never build with it.

mā in front of a past verb is the second fossil. mā qalla wa dalla keeps a shape ordinary speech no longer uses in this position, and it too is stored as one string. Bare mā is not this module's to define.

hunāka mathal yaqūl and kamā yaqūl al-mathal are the two frames that mark what follows as a quotation. Both stand on L3-M5's yaqūl, unchanged, and both are the safest way for a learner to deploy a saying at all.

REGISTER is the real trap. An English proverb in conversation is usually jokey or ironic; an Arabic proverb is graver and borrows the authority of everyone who said it before you. It is not a punchline.

L4-M5's ka- and the free-standing mithl both mean like, and both make a LIVE comparison: khafīfa ka-al-ʿuṣfūr is about actual lightness. khafīf ad-damm looks like the same shape and is not a comparison at all.

sentences.display: hunāka mathal yaqūl: man jadda wajada
sentences.script: هناك مثل يقول: من جد وجد
sentences.cue: There is a proverb that says: he who strives, finds.
sentences.literal: There a-proverb it-says: whoever strove, found

words.note: The word for a proverb; the plural is amthāl. With the article, al-mathal, it is what the quoting frame names: kamā yaqūl al-mathal.
One stored string. The man here is not L2-M7's question word who — it is a fossil free relative that lives only inside sayings.

sentences.trap: man is L2-M7's who as a question. Inside a proverb it means whoever, and it is not a rule you may build with — ordinary Arabic does not open a relative clause this way.
sentences.sound: man JAD-da wa-JA-da: both verbs hold a doubled middle consonant, and the two rhyme. A proverb is shaped to be repeated.

variations.display: hunāka mathal yaqūl: aṣ-ṣabr miftāḥ al-faraj
variations.script: هناك مثل يقول: الصبر مفتاح الفرج
variations.cue: There is a proverb that says: patience is the key to relief.
variations.changed: the proverb inside the frame; the frame itself never moves

variations.display: yaqūl abī dāʾiman: man jadda wajada
variations.script: يقول أبي دائمًا: من جد وجد
variations.cue: My father always says: he who strives, finds.
variations.changed: who is quoting it — the saying is untouched, as a saying must be

mistake.why: Modernising the proverb into the present destroys it. A saying is stored, not conjugated: the past-plus-past shape is the fossil, and changing it leaves the words true and the proverb gone.

sentences.usage: Introducing a proverb you are about to quote — the safest way for a learner to use one at all.
sentences.mnemonic: A proverb is quoted, never conjugated.

sentences.display: mā qalla wa dalla, kamā yaqūl al-mathal
sentences.script: ما قل ودل، كما يقول المثل
sentences.cue: Brief and to the point, as the proverb says.
sentences.literal: What was-little and pointed, as says the-proverb

words.note: Stored whole. The mā sits in front of a past verb in a way ordinary speech no longer uses; the phrase praises something said shortly and well.
The quoting frame's as. It stands in front of a verb and leaves it alone: L3-M5's yaqūl is unchanged behind it.

sentences.trap: Four words, and not one of them is doing its ordinary job. Do not try to build with mā plus a past verb — outside a saying the course negates a past with L3-M4's lam.
sentences.sound: mā QAL-la wa DAL-la: two doubled verbs and an internal rhyme. The shape is how you know a saying has landed.

variations.display: mā qalla wa dalla, kamā yaqūl abī
variations.script: ما قل ودل، كما يقول أبي
variations.cue: Brief and to the point, as my father says.
variations.changed: who is credited with the saying

variations.display: hunāka mathal yaqūl: mā qalla wa dalla
variations.script: هناك مثل يقول: ما قل ودل
variations.cue: There is a proverb that says: brief and to the point.
variations.changed: the other frame, which moves in front of the saying

mistake.why: Rebuilding the saying with the ordinary past negative gives grammatical Arabic and no proverb. A fossil is not a pattern; it is a string.

sentences.usage: Praising something said briefly and well — a short speech, a short answer, a short message.
sentences.mnemonic: Short, and it lands: mā qalla wa dalla.

sentences.display: aṣ-ṣabr miftāḥ al-faraj, wa hādhā mathal qadīm
sentences.script: الصبر مفتاح الفرج، وهذا مثل قديم
sentences.cue: Patience is the key to relief, and this is an old proverb.
sentences.literal: The-patience key the-relief, and this proverb old

words.note: Patience as a thing, so it carries the article. The proverb is a nominal sentence — subject, predicate, and no verb between them.

words.cue: relief, the lifting of a hardship
words.note: Not happiness: the moment a difficulty ends. L1-M7's miftāḥ, a key, is doing figurative work in front of it.
Of things, not of people — a proverb, a house, a story. An old person is kabīr fī as-sinn, which is L4-M8's.

sentences.trap: The English is patience IS the key; the Arabic has no is. Four levels in, the missing copula still catches learners inside a saying, where there is no verb to lean on.
sentences.sound: aṣ-ṣABR: sun-letter assimilation, so the l of al- is not said — aṣ-ṣabr, never al-ṣabr. miftāḥ carries a long ā.

variations.display: aṣ-ṣabr miftāḥ al-faraj, kamā yaqūl al-mathal
variations.script: الصبر مفتاح الفرج، كما يقول المثل
variations.cue: Patience is the key to relief, as the proverb says.
variations.changed: the comment becomes the quoting frame

variations.cue: This is a very old proverb.
variations.changed: only the comment survives; the proverb itself is dropped

mistake.why: Every added word is grammatical and the proverb is gone. A saying is quoted with the words it has; padding it out reads as someone explaining it rather than saying it.

sentences.usage: Said to someone waiting out a hard stretch — a delay, an illness, an application.
sentences.mnemonic: Patience is a key, not a wait.

sentences.cue: My friend is very good company.

words.note: Light of blood. The iḍāfa is L3's and the meaning is not: the whole says pleasant to be around, and no part of it says that.

sentences.trap: Word for word this is a blood disorder. The idiom is stored whole and translated whole; taking khafīf and ad-damm apart gives you nothing the sentence means.
sentences.sound: kha-FĪF ad-DAMM: kh is the throat-clearing sound, and the article assimilates to the sun letter d, so the m of damm is doubled and held.

variations.cue: My father is good company.
variations.changed: who is being described

variations.cue: The manager is good company too.
variations.changed: ayḍan adds the idiom to somebody already mentioned

mistake.why: The same words in another order. A fixed expression exists in one order only, and an idiom has no variants a learner may invent.

sentences.usage: The warmest ordinary compliment about a person's company — a friend, a colleague, a host.

sentences.display: jārī ṭawīl al-bāl, wa huwa khafīf ad-damm ayḍan
sentences.script: جاري طويل البال، وهو خفيف الدم أيضًا
sentences.cue: My neighbour is patient, and he is good company too.
sentences.literal: My-neighbour long the-mind, and he light the-blood also

words.note: Neighbour. With -ī on the end it is my neighbour; al-jār is the form the proverb al-jār qabla ad-dār uses.
Long of mind. ṭawīl is L2-M2's long, al-bāl the mind as a place where things wait — and the whole simply means patient.

sentences.trap: Two body idioms side by side, and neither can be read through its parts. English has the same habit — thick-skinned, warm-hearted — so the idea transfers even though no single idiom does.
sentences.sound: JĀ-rī ṭa-WĪL al-BĀL: three long ā vowels in a row, and al-bāl keeps the l of the article because b is a moon letter.

variations.cue: The manager is patient.
variations.changed: who is patient

variations.cue: My neighbour is always patient.
variations.changed: dāʾiman makes it a standing trait rather than today's mood

mistake.why: An idiom does not take an extra adjective inside it. Anything else you want to say about the person goes in a second clause, as wa huwa khafīf ad-damm ayḍan does here.

sentences.usage: Describing someone who does not lose their temper — a teacher, a driver, a parent.

sentences.display: hunāka mathal yaqūl: al-jār qabla ad-dār
sentences.script: هناك مثل يقول: الجار قبل الدار
sentences.cue: There is a proverb that says: the neighbour before the house.
sentences.literal: There a-proverb it-says: the-neighbour before the-house

words.note: The older word for a house, kept alive by this proverb and by its rhyme with al-jār. The everyday word is L1-M3's al-bayt.

sentences.trap: It is advice, not a statement of fact: find out who lives next door before you buy. English keeps the same advice as a whole sentence; Arabic keeps it as four words.
sentences.sound: al-JĀR QAB-la ad-DĀR: jār and dār rhyme, and the rhyme is why the saying survived at all.

variations.display: al-jār qabla ad-dār, kamā yaqūl al-mathal
variations.script: الجار قبل الدار، كما يقول المثل
variations.cue: The neighbour before the house, as the proverb says.
variations.changed: the frame moves behind the saying

variations.cue: My father says: the neighbour before the house.
variations.changed: a person quotes it instead of the frame

mistake.why: al-bayt is the everyday word and the proverb does not take it. Swapping the synonym in kills the rhyme, and a saying with its rhyme gone stops being heard as a saying.

sentences.usage: Said when somebody is choosing where to live, or explaining why they stayed where they are.
sentences.mnemonic: jār before dār — the rhyme is the rule.

sentences.display: ʿuṣfūr fī al-yad khayr min ʿuṣfūr ʿalā ash-shajara
sentences.script: عصفور في اليد خير من عصفور على الشجرة
sentences.cue: A bird in the hand is better than a bird in the tree.
sentences.literal: A-bird in the-hand better than a-bird on the-tree

words.note: A small bird. With L4-M5's ka- joined on the front it makes ka-al-ʿuṣfūr, like a bird, which is the comparison two sentences below.
Tree. sh is a sun letter, so the article assimilates and it is written and said ash-shajara.

sentences.trap: This one really does transfer: English says a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, and the Arabic says almost the same words. That is rare, and it is not a licence — most idioms carried across come out as nonsense.
sentences.sound: ʿuṣ-FŪR: the ʿ is the tight throat sound, not the hamza. ʿalā ash-SHA-ja-ra assimilates the article to the sh.

variations.display: al-ʿuṣfūr fī al-yad khayr min ʿuṣfūr ʿalā ash-shajara
variations.script: العصفور في اليد خير من عصفور على الشجرة
variations.cue: The bird in the hand is better than a bird in the tree.
variations.changed: the article on the first bird; the saying is quoted both ways

variations.display: hunāka mathal yaqūl: ʿuṣfūr fī al-yad khayr min ʿuṣfūr ʿalā ash-shajara
variations.script: هناك مثل يقول: عصفور في اليد خير من عصفور على الشجرة
variations.cue: There is a proverb that says: a bird in the hand is better than a bird in the tree.
variations.changed: the quoting frame in front, which is how a learner should introduce it

mistake.display: ʿuṣfūr fī al-yad khayr min ʿuṣfūrayn fī ash-shajara
mistake.script: عصفور في اليد خير من عصفورين في الشجرة
mistake.why: Importing the English arithmetic — two in the bush — gives a dual this ladder has not taught and a proverb Arabic does not say. Quote the Arabic saying, not a translation of yours.

sentences.usage: Arguing for taking what is already on the table — a job, a price, a date already agreed.
sentences.mnemonic: One in the hand beats one on the branch.

sentences.cue: She is as light as a bird.

words.note: The plain adjective, meaning light. It is the same word as in khafīf ad-damm, where nothing about it is literal — one adjective, two jobs.
The free-standing like, where L4-M5's ka- is a clitic written joined. mithl al-ʿuṣfūr and ka-al-ʿuṣfūr are the same comparison.

sentences.trap: Here the comparison is literal — a real bird, real lightness. The trap runs the other way: khafīf ad-damm looks like the same construction and is a stored idiom, not a comparison you may extend.
sentences.sound: kha-FĪ-fa ka-al-ʿuṣ-FŪR: ka- is written joined to what it compares, so the whole comparison is one written word with its stress at the end.

variations.cue: She is as light as a bird.
variations.changed: ka- becomes the free-standing mithl; the meaning does not move

variations.cue: He is as light as a bird.
variations.changed: the gender, so the adjective loses its -a

mistake.why: Two systems welded together. khafīf ad-damm is a stored idiom about company, ka-al-ʿuṣfūr a live comparison about weight; running them into one sentence says neither.

sentences.usage: An ordinary compliment about someone's step, or about a child.
sentences.mnemonic: ka- is glued on; mithl stands alone.

sentences.display: hādhā ar-rajul ṭawīl al-lisān wa lākin qalbuhu abyaḍ
sentences.script: هذا الرجل طويل اللسان ولكن قلبه أبيض
sentences.cue: This man is sharp-tongued, but he is kind-hearted.
sentences.literal: This the-man long the-tongue and but his-heart white

words.note: Long of tongue — the same iḍāfa shape as ṭawīl al-bāl and the opposite verdict. Fixed whole: swapping the body part does not give you a new idiom.
Heart, with -hu for his. qalbuhu abyaḍ — his heart is white — is the idiom for kind.
White. Inside this idiom it carries clean and kind; the colour English reaches for is a temperature instead, and the two do not swap.

sentences.trap: English gives kindness a temperature — warm-hearted — and Arabic gives it a colour. Translating warm across produces nothing; the idiom is stored with its own colour.
sentences.sound: ṭa-WĪL al-li-SĀN: l is a sun letter, so the article's l runs into it and doubles — al-lisān. Then QAL-bu-hu AB-yaḍ.

variations.cue: This man is sharp-tongued.
variations.changed: the concession is dropped and only the complaint is left

variations.display: al-mudīr ṭawīl al-lisān, wa lākin qalbuhu abyaḍ
variations.script: المدير طويل اللسان، ولكن قلبه أبيض
variations.cue: The manager is sharp-tongued, but he is kind-hearted.
variations.changed: who is being described

mistake.why: Warm-hearted translated straight across. sākhin is heat, and about a heart it says nothing a speaker recognises — the idiom needs abyaḍ.

sentences.usage: Excusing someone whose manner is harsh — a relative, a boss, an old friend.

sentences.cue: It's a small world, as the proverb says.

words.note: The world as the place people live in, and it always takes the article. ad-dunyā ṣaghīra is what you say on running into someone unexpectedly.

sentences.trap: The saying lands exactly where English puts it's a small world, which makes it the easiest item here — and the register is still graver: it is said with a shrug at how things fall out, not as a joke.
sentences.sound: ad-DUN-yā ṣa-GHĪ-ra: sun-letter d doubles after the article, and the final -ā of dunyā is long.

variations.cue: It's a very small world.
variations.changed: jiddan intensifies it, which this saying tolerates

variations.cue: There is a proverb that says: it's a small world.
variations.changed: the frame in front

mistake.why: A literal translation of small world. It is understandable and it is not the saying; ad-dunyā is the word the fixed expression uses and the one a listener is waiting for.

sentences.usage: On meeting someone you know in an unexpected place.
